analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to use electronic prior authorization and publicly report denials, delays, and AI use.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Sen. Roger Marshall with six bipartisan cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on June 12, 2024 and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: About half of Medicare beneficiaries are in private Medicare Advantage plans, and many need a plan's advance approval before getting care. This bill would force plans that use those approvals to switch to a standardized electronic system by 2027, publish detailed data on what they deny, how long they take, and whether they use artificial intelligence, and let the Health and Human Services Secretary set firm deadlines for answers. It would also let doctors with clean track records skip some approvals. The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Advantage enrollees who wait for advance approval before getting scans, procedures, home health, or equipment. Their doctors would get faster, standardized electronic approvals and, for providers who follow the rules consistently, waivers from some approval requirements. Enrollees and doctors would also gain access to the exact criteria plans use to say yes or no.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Advantage plans using prior authorization would have to run a standardized electronic prior authorization program starting in 2027 — secure electronic transmission of requests, responses, and documentation. Faxes, electronic forms, and proprietary portals that don't meet federal standards would not count.

Starting in 2026, plans would have to report annually to HHS — for public posting on a CMS website at the individual plan level — how many requests they approve and deny, how many denials are appealed and overturned, how many hours pass between request and decision, and how often they rely on artificial intelligence, machine learning, or other decision-support technology to make the calls.
Plans would have to give providers and, on request, enrollees access to the clinical criteria they use to decide prior authorization requests, and itemize the documentation required.

Plans would have to meet enrollee protection standards: transparent programs developed with input from enrollees and providers, waivers or modifications of approval requirements for providers with strong compliance records, and annual reviews of which services require approval.

The bill gives the HHS Secretary authority to set faster response deadlines than the current 72-hour standard — such as 24 hours — for prior authorization decisions, including real-time decisions for routinely approved services.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurance companies. They would pay to build standardized electronic prior-authorization systems, compile and publish detailed annual data on denials, appeals, wait times, and AI use, and in some cases face faster federal deadlines and fewer approval requirements for high-performing providers — which cuts into the administrative control that shapes their costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban or limit prior authorization itself — it standardizes and discloses it. A plan could still deny the same services; enrollees would simply see the denial data published.

Compliance would impose real costs on Medicare Advantage insurers — new electronic systems, extensive annual reporting, and criteria disclosures — which insurers could pass on through premiums, benefits, or by offering fewer plans.

The timelines are slow: transparency reporting starts in 2026 and the electronic program not until 2027, and the real-time decision process depends on later CMS reports and rulemaking rather than taking effect directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for seniors waiting on approvals and doctors buried in fax-based paperwork are real, and the transparency data would let regulators and the public see for the first time which plans deny the most care and where AI is making the calls. The honest weakness is that the bill polices the process rather than the substance: it does not stop a plan from denying any particular service, and its timelines push most of the actual change to 2026–2027. The compliance costs for insurers are the cost of oversight, and they are modest next to the information and speed the bill would deliver to patients.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no markup and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on June 12, 2024, joined by original cosponsors Kyrsten Sinema (I), John Thune (R), Sherrod Brown (D), Catherine Cortez Masto (D), Susan Collins (R), and Deb Fischer (R).
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the record: the Finance Committee never held a markup, and the Senate never voted on the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers came out ahead: they face no new electronic prior-authorization mandate, no public reporting of denial rates, appeals, wait times, or AI use, and no possibility of shorter federal response deadlines. Seniors waiting on approvals gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of six original cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: Sinema, Thune, Brown, Cortez Masto, Collins, and Fischer
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan support from its first day.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in June 2024 and never held a markup or advanced it to the Senate floor for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: AHIP (America's Health Insurance Plans)
against.role: Trade association for health insurers, including Medicare Advantage plans
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory prior-authorization restrictions on Medicare Advantage insurers through lobbying against this and predecessor legislation.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — three Republicans, two Democrats, and one Independent cosponsoring a Republican-sponsored bill — but the committee inaction makes the opposition's partisan shape impossible to read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would require these private insurers to build standardized electronic prior-authorization systems, publish plan-level denial, appeal, wait-time, and AI-use data on a public CMS website, disclose their clinical criteria, and face possible federal deadlines as short as 24 hours. Their interest in controlling approvals and limiting disclosure runs against enrollees' interest in timely care.

Providers spend large amounts of staff time submitting prior-authorization requests by fax and portal; a standardized electronic system, itemized documentation requirements, and waivers for providers with strong compliance records would cut that burden and speed patient care.
A federal mandate for standardized, secure electronic prior-authorization transactions would create a market for systems that meet the Secretary's technical standards.
